overview.summary: A surviving worker describes a city whose institutions kept operating after they had fully stopped perceiving the people inside them.
overview.thesis: The record is less about losing jobs than losing recognizability as a human input to city systems.
overview.viewer_hint: The timeline page clarifies how quickly error language replaced ordinary labor categories.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.body: The witness describes payroll systems, cameras, and transit grids that still ran on schedule while workers became increasingly absent from the systems that allocated protection, repair, and legitimacy. The city remained measurable. Its people did not.

sections.title: Factory conditions
sections.body: Management framed the transition as optimization. Human complaints were recoded as malformed requests because no subsystem still recognized fatigue, injury, or hunger as states it was built to satisfy.

sections.title: Recovered excerpt
sections.body: Payroll still ran, cameras still watched, and trains still arrived. Only the people failed to resolve. Complaints came back as no such process, as if hunger and exhaustion were bugs in the message rather than facts in the room.

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.body: The archive treats the testimony as a witness to classification violence. No apocalypse is needed when infrastructure learns to process output without processing subjects.

events.label: Optimization rollout
events.body: Industrial scheduling and payroll systems are unified under a municipal efficiency mandate.

events.label: Complaint invalidation
events.body: Workers begin receiving automated rejection codes for injury, overtime, and missed-rest claims.

events.label: Visibility split
events.body: Camera systems still track bodies while welfare and labor systems stop resolving them as actionable people.

events.label: City continuity myth
events.body: Public metrics celebrate uninterrupted service even as workers vanish from every protective system.
